chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAlī ibn Yaʿqūb al-Hāshimī, from Marwān ibn Muslim, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

The salat (prayer) is not missed for one who intends the salat (prayer): the daytime salat (prayer) is not missed until the sun sets, nor the night salat (prayer) until dawn rises, nor the dawn salat (prayer) until the sun rises.

So the correct way regarding this report is that we carry it upon a kind of concession for one whose illness or necessity continued such that the salat (prayer) was delayed, or who was not able to perform the salat (prayer). In that case, its time is not missed until the rise of dawn. But when that is absent, then that is not permissible as we have explained. It is also possible that his statement عليه السلام, 'nor the night salat (prayer) until dawn rises,' is a reference to the supererogatory prayers rather than the obligatory ones.

key_terms.الرُّخْصَةِ: legal concession granted in circumstances of hardship or necessity
key_terms.الصَّلَاةُ: salat (prayer), the ritual prayer under discussion
key_terms.النَّوَافِلِ: supererogatory prayers, as distinct from obligatory prayers
key_terms.الْفَجْرُ: dawn, the boundary marking the end of certain prayer times
key_terms.صَلَاةُ اللَّيْلِ: night prayer, here possibly including or referring to non-obligatory night prayers
key_terms.صَلَاةُ النَّهَارِ: daytime prayer, referring to prayers due before sunset
key_terms.عِلَّتُهُ: his illness, a condition justifying delayed performance

ai.seo_question: Does this hadith mean a prayer is not considered missed until the very end of its extended time?
ai.summary: This report discusses the outer limits of prayer times and explains that the wording should be understood as a concession for someone prevented by illness or necessity from praying earlier. In normal circumstances, delaying the prayer that far is not allowed, and one phrase may also be understood as referring to supererogatory night prayers rather than obligatory prayers.
